notes.meaning: Moses begins this prayer by declaring that the Lord has always been the true home and shelter for His people. Even when Israel lived in tents and wandered in the desert, God provided safety across every generation. Believers find their ultimate security not in buildings or earthly places, but in God Himself.

Long before the ancient mountains were formed and the earth was created, God already existed. He has no beginning and no end, but is God from everlasting to everlasting. While everything in creation changes and wears out, God remains completely stable and faithful.

God commands mortal humans to return to the dust from which they were made. Human beings were originally created for life, but sin brought the sentence of physical death upon everyone. God alone holds sovereign authority over human life and its end.

To an eternal God, a thousand years pass like a single day that is already gone, or like a three-hour watch in the middle of the night. Humans feel that time moves slowly, but God stands above time entirely. This reminds us not to judge God's timing or patience by our short life spans.

Human lives are swept away suddenly, like people carried off in a flash flood or waking from a quick dream. We are compared to morning grass that shoots up fresh and green, but by evening is cut down and completely dried up. Life on earth is fragile and swift, reminding us to rely on what is eternal.

The people confess that their lives are worn away and terrified by God's righteous anger. In the wilderness, Israel experienced the painful reality of dying off because of their rebellion against the Lord. Sickness, trouble, and physical death show how serious it is to break covenant with God.

God sets all of human wrongdoing right before His eyes, exposing even secret sins under the bright light of His presence. Nothing done in private or hidden in darkness can escape His notice as a holy judge. Because God sees everything clearly, our only hope is to seek His forgiveness rather than try to hide our faults.

Under the shadow of divine judgment, human days fade away quickly and end like a quiet sigh or fading groan. Human plans and operations are fragile, and life often closes with sadness rather than earthly triumph. Recognizing how quickly our years slip away leads us to seek God's enduring mercy.

A typical human lifetime reaches about seventy years, or perhaps eighty if a person has unusual strength. Even the years people boast about are filled with hard toil, weakness, and sorrow. Time rushes forward quickly, and soon we fly away from this earthly life.

The psalmist asks who can truly grasp the overwhelming power of God's anger against sin. God's wrath is as great as the deep reverence and holy fear that He rightfully deserves. Standing in healthy awe of God keeps us from treating sin lightly.

Moses prays for God to teach His people to number their days so they can develop wise hearts. This does not mean predicting the future, but realizing how brief life is and taking every day seriously. True wisdom comes when we give our short lives over to honoring God.

The prayer turns from lament to a cry for the Lord to return and show pity to His servants. Moses asks how long God's severe chastisement will continue and pleads for a change in His dealings. God invites His people to ask boldly for His compassion during seasons of affliction.

The people ask God to satisfy them early and promptly with His loyal, steadfast love. Like the bright dawn following a long night of distress, God's mercy brings lasting gladness. Only God's loving-kindness can fill the human heart with true joy that lasts for a lifetime.

The psalmist asks God to give seasons of joy that match the length and depth of the hardships they endured. After decades of wandering and suffering in the wilderness, the people long for an equal measure of divine blessing. We can look to God to restore gladness after long seasons of pain.

Moses asks the Lord to show His mighty saving deeds to His current servants and reveal His glory to their children. This looks forward to God fulfilling His promises by caring for future generations. Believers pray not only for God's blessings in their own lifetime, but also for their children to witness His majesty.

The psalm closes with a plea for the Lord's favor and beauty to rest upon His people. The writer repeats the request for God to establish the work of their hands so their efforts will last. Human work only succeeds and bears fruit when God gives it strength and purpose.
